title: Pando: Earth’s Oldest, Hugest Organism Is Trees!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Pando, a quaking aspen clone in Utah's Fishlake area of the Colorado Front Range (as the hosts describe it) covering about 106 acres and estimated at 13,000 to 80,000 years old, possibly far older. They cover aspen biology (living bark that photosynthesizes, leaf sound, vegetative and sexual reproduction, male sex of Pando), how fire helps aspen regenerate and how conifers crowd them out, and why Pando is declining due to overbrowsing by mule deer and elk, human development and campgrounds, and fire suppression. A Forest Service fenced exclosure from 2013 showed regrowth. Other ancient organisms are mentioned (Armillaria mushroom in Oregon, bristlecone pines, creosote bush, glass sponges). The episode closes with listener mail about Robin Hood and Sherwood Forest's Major Oak.

segments.title: Introduction and aspen basics
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce Pando and describe quaking aspens: size, bark with chlorophyll, leaves and the distinctive trembling sound.

segments.title: What Pando is: a genetically identical clone
segments.summary: Pando is a roughly 106-acre stand of genetically identical quaking aspens connected by one root system and described as the largest organism on Earth, weighing about 13 million pounds. The hosts explain vegetative reproduction via root suckers, clones, and that Pando is male.

segments.title: Resource sharing within the clone
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how connected trees share water and resources through the shared root system and how aspens spread across North America.

segments.title: Fire and aspen regeneration
segments.summary: Aspens resist burning but sprout vigorously after wildfire, which suppresses conifers. Conifers burn and are outcompeted, and aspen can dominate for decades to centuries. Fire suppression by humans is discussed.

segments.title: Identifying clones and genetic testing
segments.summary: Early researchers identified clones by fall leaf color; genetic testing showed some assumptions were wrong, including a supposed sex change that turned out to be two different clones.

segments.title: Age and immortality of aspen clones
segments.summary: Individual aspen stems live about 75 to 200 years, while Pando is estimated at 13,000 to 80,000 years old, with a University of Michigan estimate of up to a million mentioned as a joke. Clones may be essentially immortal in principle.

segments.title: Why Pando is declining
segments.summary: Pando is dying due to human development, campgrounds, overbrowsing by mule deer and elk, lack of young saplings, and a 2013 Forest Service fenced exclosure study. Paul Rodgers of Utah State University is discussed, along with the wildlife management dispute over hunting licenses and the role of wolves, bears and mountain lions in an ecology of fear.

segments.title: Other ancient organisms
segments.summary: The hosts mention a giant Armillaria mushroom in Mallard National Forest in Oregon, bristlecone pines, a creosote bush, and glass sponges as other very old or large organisms.

segments.title: Listener mail: Robin Hood and Sherwood Forest
segments.summary: A listener from Nottingham writes about the Major Oak in Sherwood Forest and the hosts' Robin Hood episode, and offers the hosts band shirts.
